title: Sessions, sandbox lifecycle and state
summary: Compute follows the session, not the request. Each session gets a VM-isolated sandbox that moves between Active, Idle and Resumed, with `$HOME` and `/files` persisted across idle periods and deleted after 30 days of inactivity.
useIf: You are designing where a hosted agent keeps working files, history and checkpoints, and how long they live.
avoidIf: You run a prompt agent, where the platform owns conversation state and you have no sandbox to manage.

explain.md: A **session ID** names a logical session with persisted state. The platform provisions compute on demand and restores the state onto it [[r2]]. Each session has its own VM-isolated sandbox with a persistent filesystem (`$HOME` and `/files`), which gives scale-to-zero with stateful resume and predictable cold starts [[r2]]. Files uploaded through `/files` land in `$HOME`. State is persisted when a session goes idle and restored on resume [[r2]].

explain.title: Session lifecycle
explain.alt: A session is Active while handling requests, becomes Idle after the idle timeout with state persisted, is Resumed on the next request, and is deleted after 30 days idle.
explain.src:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Active: first request
  Active --> Idle: idle timeout, state persisted
  Idle --> Resumed: next request, state restored
  Resumed --> Idle: idle timeout
  Idle --> [*]: deleted after 30 days idle

items.label: Sandbox sizes
items.note: 0.5 vCPU 1 GiB, 1 vCPU 2 GiB, 2 vCPU 4 GiB [[r2]]

items.label: Disk budget
items.note: At 1 vCPU or larger, about 20 percent reserved, shared with the image and `$HOME` [[r2]]

explain.md: Besides the filesystem there is a **durable key-value state store** that survives crashes and idle eviction, can be partitioned per end user, and ages items out after a 30 day idle window by default [[r2]]. With the Responses protocol the platform keeps conversation history by conversation ID. With Invocations you manage sessions yourself [[r2]].

explain.title: Long-running resilience (preview, checked 2026-10-13)
explain.md: Background execution lets work continue after the request returns. Resilient execution lets a later process recover work after a crash or restart. They solve different problems [[tr2]]. Recovery **reenters the handler from its beginning**. It is not deterministic replay and does not restore local variables, so the handler must use durable checkpoints, idempotency keys or watermarks. Full crash recovery for Responses applies only to stored background responses that opt in [[tr2]].

whereToUse: Agents that keep a working directory, downloaded files or caches across turns
Per-user workspaces where each end user maps to one session or state-store partition
Long extraction or research jobs that must survive a restart (preview resilience features)
Choosing idle timeouts per version to trade resume latency against active-session cost

use: Use `$HOME` for files that belong to one session and may sit idle for a while
Use the state store for small key-value state that must outlive a crash
Use external storage you own for anything that must outlive 30 idle days or be shared across sessions
avoid: Do not rely on in-memory variables or paths outside `$HOME` and `/files` surviving idle (inference from what is documented as persisted)
Do not treat the session as a database: it is deleted after 30 days of inactivity
Do not size the sandbox for the whole agent: the cpu and memory you set describe one session, and billing multiplies by active sessions
flips: Data must be shared between users or sessions: move it to external storage
Resume latency hurts the user experience: raise the idle timeout, accepting more active-session time
A job outlives a single process: add resilient execution and idempotent checkpoints

pitfalls.symptom: A user returns after five weeks and the workspace files are gone
pitfalls.cause: The session was permanently deleted after 30 days of inactivity
pitfalls.fix: Keep long-lived data in storage you own and treat session state as a cache [[r2]].

pitfalls.symptom: After a crash the agent sends a duplicate email or payment
pitfalls.cause: Recovery reenters the handler from the beginning
pitfalls.fix: Persist an idempotency key or side-effect watermark before the unsafe call and check it on re-entry [[tr2]].

pitfalls.symptom: Sandbox runs out of disk with a small image
pitfalls.cause: The disk budget is shared with the image and `$HOME` and about 20 percent is reserved
pitfalls.fix: Right-size the tier, prune uploads and offload large artifacts to storage [[r2]].

scenarios.title: Per-user data that must last 90 days
scenarios.situation: A hosted agent builds a per-user knowledge workspace. Users come back every few weeks and the data must remain for 90 days after the last visit.
constraints: Data may be shared across a user's sessions
unknowns: Is the data sensitive or regulated?
scenarios.question: Where does the workspace live?

options.name: External database or blob storage keyed by user
options.why: It outlives the 30 day session deletion and the 30 day state-store aging, and it can be shared across sessions.
options.tradeoff: You build access control, backup and RBAC for the agent identity.

options.name: Durable key-value state store partitioned per user
options.why: Survives crashes and idle eviction and partitions per end user.
options.tradeoff: Items age out after a 30 day idle window by default, so it does not meet 90 days without checking configuration.

options.name: Files in `$HOME`
options.why: The session is deleted after 30 days of inactivity, taking `$HOME` with it.
options.tradeoff: Right for working files that only matter during an active engagement.

flips.if: Retention only needs to be 14 days
flips.then: The state store or `$HOME` becomes acceptable and simpler.
External storage with your own retention and deletion controls.

scenarios.takeaway: Session state is a cache with a 30 day horizon, not a system of record.

scenarios.title: Forty-minute job that sometimes crashes
scenarios.situation: A document extraction run takes about forty minutes and occasionally dies from memory pressure. Clients disconnect while it runs.
constraints: Steps call an external API that must not be repeated
scenarios.question: How do you design for recovery?

options.name: Resilient execution with durable checkpoints and idempotency keys
options.why: Recovery reenters the handler with the same identities, and checkpoints plus watermarks skip finished work and the unsafe call.
options.tradeoff: Preview, and you must write the resume logic.

options.name: Background mode only
options.why: It keeps work going after the request returns but does not recover after the owning process stops.
options.tradeoff: Right for work that is cheap to rerun or tolerates loss.

options.name: Foreground call with a client retry
options.why: Simple, and a retry reruns from the start.
options.tradeoff: Repeats forty minutes of work and may repeat the external call.

flips.if: The job takes seconds and is safe to rerun

flips.then: Own the recovery in your framework checkpointer and an external job store.

scenarios.takeaway: Background is not resilience, and recovery restarts the handler, so design for idempotency.

quiz.q: Order the documented life of a hosted agent session.
items: A request arrives and the sandbox is Active
The idle timeout fires and `$HOME` and `/files` are persisted
A later request restores state and the session is Resumed
After 30 days of inactivity the session is permanently deleted
quiz.explain: Active comes first, idle persists state, resume restores it, and deletion happens only after 30 inactive days.

quiz.q: At 1 vCPU the disk budget is up to 20 GiB with about 20 percent reserved. About how many GiB remain to share between the image and `$HOME`?
quiz.explain: Reserve about 4 GiB (20 percent of 20), leaving about 16 GiB. This is derived from the documented figures, so treat it as an estimate.

quiz.q: After a crash a recovered handler repeats a non-idempotent call. What is the cause?
options: The idle timeout is too short
Recovery reenters the handler from the beginning and the handler had no watermark
The session was resumed on a larger sandbox
quiz.explain: Resilient recovery is not deterministic replay. The handler restarts from its beginning and must use checkpoints or watermarks. Idle timeout and sandbox size are unrelated.

flashcards.front: What is persisted when a hosted agent session goes idle?
flashcards.back: `$HOME` and `/files` content. State is restored on resume. The session is deleted after 30 days of inactivity.
Background keeps work running after the request returns. Resilience lets a later process recover it after a crash. Recovery restarts the handler, so use checkpoints (preview).
